newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgian-Abkhaz talks make little headway-official.
newsitem.headline: Georgian-Abkhaz talks make little headway-official.

text.p: Two weeks of intense peace talks between Georgia and its secessionist-minded Abkhazia region have ended with little progress made, raising fears of possible renewed conflict between the two sides.
The failure comes as a deadline for the withdrawal of a contingent of Russian peacekeepers looms just five weeks away.

Georgian Deputy Foreign Minister Giga Burduli said the talks this week in Moscow between Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba and Georgian Foreign Minister Irakly Menagarishvili, had brought only minor progress.
"The negotiations have ended for now. There is some convergence of our positions, but it is not major," he told Reuters. He said the thorny question of Abkhazia's status remained unsolved.

The Abkhaz say they want independence or a "union state" of two equal partners. Georgia has rejected this, saying it would give the lush subtropical province international rights that it could later use to get full independence. Tbilisi is offering wide autonomy instead.

"Abkhazia has made a maximum of compromises," Ardzinba told Interfax news agency in Moscow before leaving for his capital Sukhumi. He said that the two sides had worked on a wide-ranging political agreement but that now "it is completely up to the Georgian side" as to whether it can be concluded.

Abkhazia, once favored by the Soviet Union's rich and famous, has run itself as an independent state since its fighters, with volunteers and military support from Russia, evicted Georgian troops sent in to stop moves for more autonomy.

But Abkhazia's de facto sovereignty has been eerily lonely. No state has recognized it, and a partial blockade enforced by Russia and Georgia has destroyed the economy, left the once-lively beaches empty and most Abkhaz living from hand to mouth. Travel to and from the region is next to impossible.
Georgia says it has lost patience with the Abkhaz after three years of fruitless peace talks, with 2,500 Russian peacekeepers patrolling a buffer zone between the two sides.

It has demanded the peacekeepers leave after July 31 unless they begin patrolling a larger part of Abkhazia and help resettle some of the at least 150,000 Georgian refugees from the conflict who have still not been able to go home.

The wider mandate was approved by the leaders of the former Soviet republics grouped in the Commonwealth of Independent States earlier this year but Russia says it wants Abkhazia to agree to the changes as well. Abkhazia is bitterly opposed.
A Russian withdrawal would leave a vacuum which observers say could lead to a reignition of fighting which killed more than 10,000 people in 1992-93.
Furthermore, Georgia has scheduled what it says will be its largest military exercises ever close to the de facto frontier with Abkhazia for July.

President Eduard Shevardnadze says he has no intention of launching a new assault to recapture the region, but has warned that the Abkhaz side would be commiting "suicide" if it chose to go to war with his rebuilt army.
An aide to Shevardnadze said the Russians would have to leave if they did not agree to do more by the deadline.

"People have to realise that we are not bluffing. Our patience has run out with the peacekeepers. Even if the president wants to let them stay, parliament will not allow him to do it unless they agree to our conditions," said the aide, who declined to be named.
"As for the Abkhaz, we have made every concession that any civilised state in the world can make. We are offering them a very high degree of autonomy," he said.
"There is not a single person in Georgia who could agree to what the Abkhaz are offering us right now," he said, expressing pessimism about the prospects for future negotiations.
